standard.title: Power and authority in Asia-Pacific
standard.description: the experiences and perspectives of rulers and of subject peoples, and the interaction between power and/or authority in the Asian-Pacific society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how power and authority operated in medieval European and imperial contexts (AC9HH8K04, AC9HH8K09) and the social hierarchy of the chosen Asia-Pacific society (AC9HH8K12). They have not yet analysed how power and authority specifically operated in Asia-Pacific contexts — including the Khmer god-king, the Tokugawa feudal system, or chiefly authority in Polynesian societies.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the experiences and perspectives of rulers and subject peoples in the chosen Asia-Pacific society — describing how power was exercised and legitimised, how subject peoples experienced authority, and how interactions between rulers and subjects shaped the society's development.

nodes.label: How rulers exercised authority
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how rulers in the chosen Asia-Pacific society exercised authority — including the basis of their legitimacy, the mechanisms of their rule, and how they mobilised or controlled subject peoples.
nodes.minimum_width: At least two mechanisms through which rulers exercised authority, with reference to the basis of their legitimacy.
nodes.typical_width: The mechanisms and legitimacy of rule across the chosen society. Examples: the Khmer deva-raja (god-king) enabling absolute authority through religious legitimacy — mobilising the population for defence and construction; the Tokugawa Shogunate reimposing a feudal system based on daimyo and samurai and its impact on daily life across classes; the responsibilities and privileges of chiefs (ariki) in Polynesian societies such as New Zealand, Hawaii, Tonga and the Society Islands.
wider: For the Khmer: analyse the perspectives of Angkor as depicted through stone carvings and Zhou Daguan's writings — in relation to fishing, trading and temple construction — as evidence of how royal authority shaped the lives of ordinary people

For Polynesian societies: compare the responsibilities and privileges of being a chief across different societies (Māori, Hawaiian, Tongan) to examine how chiefly authority varied in its form and functions across the Pacific
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how rulers exercised and legitimised authority is prerequisite to understanding how subject peoples experienced and responded to it. Students who cannot explain the basis of rulers' power cannot analyse the perspectives of those subject to it.

response_modes.reason: Students often focus on what rulers did without analysing why subjects accepted or submitted to their authority. Scaffold the distinction between coercive power (force) and legitimate authority (religious, hereditary, customary) and how different societies relied on different combinations.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two mechanisms through which rulers in the chosen society exercised authority
Explains the basis of the ruler's legitimacy — what gave them the right to rule in the eyes of their subjects

nodes.label: Experiences of subject peoples
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the experiences and perspectives of subject peoples in the chosen Asia-Pacific society — including how social position, class and cultural context shaped their daily life under authority.
nodes.minimum_width: A description of how authority affected the daily life of at least one subject group.
nodes.typical_width: The varied experiences of subject peoples. Examples: the impact of the Tokugawa Shogunate reimposing a feudal system on different classes (daimyo, samurai, farmers, merchants); the use of artefacts such as Lapita pottery from Vanuatu, tapa cloth and ship-building techniques to provide insight into the lives of ordinary Polynesian peoples; how daily life in the Khmer Empire was shaped by the obligations of subject peoples to the god-king.
wider: For feudal Japan: examine the impact of the Tokugawa Shogunate's reimposition of the feudal system on different classes — particularly the impact on merchants and artisans whose wealth grew but whose status remained formally low
For Polynesia: examine artefacts such as Lapita pottery, tapa cloth and ship-building techniques as evidence of the daily life and capabilities of ordinary Polynesian peoples, not just their rulers

response_modes.reason: The experience of subject peoples under authority varies dramatically across Asia-Pacific societies. Using multiple contexts (Khmer peasants vs Polynesian commoners vs Japanese samurai) prevents students from generalising from a single subordinate experience.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The contrast between the Tokugawa feudal hierarchy (rigidly codified status) and Polynesian chiefly societies (status embedded in lineage and reciprocal obligation) offers rich comparative context for understanding how different forms of authority produce different daily experiences for subject peoples.
success_criteria: Describes how authority shaped the daily life of at least one subject group in the chosen Asia-Pacific society
Identifies at least one way in which different groups within the same society experienced authority differently

nodes.label: Interactions and responses to authority
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how subject peoples responded to authority in the chosen Asia-Pacific society — including accommodation, resistance or cultural negotiation — and explain how these interactions shaped the society.
nodes.minimum_width: At least one example of how subject peoples responded to authority, with an explanation of its effect on the society.
nodes.typical_width: Responses across accommodation, resistance and exchange. Examples: how the daimyo contributed to the end of the Ashikaga Shogunate as subject-rulers challenging authority from within; the role of merchants and artisans in feudal Japan navigating formal status constraints; Polynesian peoples' practical sovereignty over resources through Rahui as a community-led response to environmental pressure; the role of councils and collective decision-making in chiefly societies.
wider: For feudal Japan: examine the role of the daimyo in contributing to the end of the Ashikaga Shogunate as a case study in how powerful subject-rulers could challenge and ultimately transform the authority structure from within

For the Khmer: examine how the god-king's authority was both sustained and undermined by his obligation to deliver prosperity — when environmental failure (drought, flooding) disrupted the water management system, the basis of royal authority was challenged

response_modes.reason: This node integrates understanding of how authority was exercised (Node 1) and experienced (Node 2) into an analysis of how the relationship between rulers and subjects was dynamic rather than fixed. Invest in helping students see authority as a relationship that required ongoing maintenance and negotiation.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one example of how subject peoples responded to authority in the chosen society
Explains how that response shaped the society — whether maintaining, modifying or challenging existing power structures
